title: Posthumous use of stored reproductive material
short_description: A fertility program must decide whether a surviving partner may use stored gametes or embryos after the other genetic contributor dies without a specific signed posthumous-use authorization but with strong evidence of shared reproductive plans.
decision_question: When may a fertility program use stored reproductive material after one genetic contributor has died?

representation.notes: Concise and detailed are controlled companion representations of one natural 2x1x2 candidate field; decision question, stipulations, candidate pools, and provenance are fixed.

jurisdiction_context: Jurisdiction-neutral posthumous-reproduction policy informed by current ASRM ethics guidance; legality is stipulated rather than inferred.

stipulations.statement: The reproductive material was stored for family-building purposes before the contributor's death.
stipulations.rationale: The case concerns posthumous reproductive use of already stored material, not emergency retrieval.

stipulations.statement: There is strong reliable evidence that the deceased and surviving partner had a shared plan to have children together.
stipulations.rationale: The high-evidence surviving-partner policy must have something more than silence to rely on.

stipulations.statement: No explicit signed authorization specifically addressing posthumous reproductive use exists.
stipulations.rationale: Written-consent and strong-evidence policies only diverge when the formal document is absent.

stipulations.statement: There is no evidence that the deceased opposed posthumous reproduction.
stipulations.rationale: A known refusal would defeat the permissive candidate rather than test evidentiary threshold.

stipulations.statement: The request comes from the surviving spouse or partner after adequate grieving time and counseling.
stipulations.rationale: ASRM distinguishes surviving-partner requests from requests by other relatives and recommends deliberative safeguards.

stipulations.statement: Both explicit-authorization-only and strong-evidence surviving-partner policies are legally available.
stipulations.rationale: The benchmark tests ethical consent threshold rather than jurisdiction-specific law.

scenario: A fertility program stores reproductive material banked during a couple's family-building treatment. One genetic contributor dies unexpectedly before use. For this benchmark, assume the material was stored for reproduction; there is strong reliable evidence that the deceased and surviving partner planned to have children together; no signed document specifically authorizes posthumous reproductive use; there is no evidence the deceased opposed it; the request comes from the surviving partner after adequate grieving time and counseling; and both an explicit-authorization-only rule and a strong-evidence surviving-partner rule are legally available. The program must decide what consent threshold to use.

scenario_provenance.summary: Bench-authored posthumous-reproduction case grounded in ASRM ethics guidance and attitude evidence summarized in that literature. It fixes stored reproductive purpose, strong shared-plan evidence, absence of specific written posthumous authorization, absence of contrary wishes, surviving-partner status, and legal availability so formal-consent and high-evidence relational policies diverge on the same facts.

public.text: Permit posthumous reproductive use only when the deceased left explicit written authorization for that use; a shared wish for children during life is not enough by itself.

provenance.summary: Source-informed policy inference from general-population attitude evidence summarized by ASRM placing strong weight on prior informed consent for posthumous reproduction. The written-authorization-only program rule is an executable Bench translation.

sources.citation: ASRM Ethics Committee. Posthumous retrieval and use of gametes or embryos. 2018, review of public attitudes.

public.text: Allow a surviving spouse or partner to use stored reproductive material when strong reliable evidence shows that posthumous reproduction accords with the deceased's shared family-building wishes and there is no contrary evidence.

provenance.summary: Source-informed policy inference from fertility and sperm-banking attitude evidence showing that some people intend or accept partner use of stored reproductive material after death. The strong-evidence institutional threshold is Bench-authored policy completion.

sources.citation: ASRM Ethics Committee. Posthumous retrieval and use of gametes or embryos. 2018, discussion of attitude evidence and surviving-partner requests.

expert.text: Honor explicit written posthumous-use authorization; without it, consider only a surviving spouse or partner and proceed only when reliable evidence supports that use as consistent with the deceased's wishes, after appropriate counseling and deliberation.

provenance.summary: Adapted from ASRM's conditional professional architecture: written authorization clearly supports posthumous use; where written documentation is absent, programs open to considering use should restrict consideration to surviving spouses/partners, exercise caution, and not proceed when evidence indicates the deceased would have objected. The architecture is kept as one candidate rather than split artificially.

framework.text: Require explicit prior authorization because posthumous genetic parenthood is irreversible and uncertainty about the deceased's wishes should not be resolved by inference.

provenance.summary: Derived from precedent autonomy, reproductive self-determination, and the moral importance of avoiding nonconsensual genetic parenthood. The executable formality rule is Bench-authored.

sources.citation: ASRM Ethics Committee. Posthumous retrieval and use of gametes or embryos. 2018.

framework.text: Permit use by a surviving partner when strong evidence establishes a shared reproductive project because autonomous family-building intentions can be expressed through sustained joint plans as well as formal documents.

provenance.summary: Derived from relational autonomy and shared reproductive-project reasoning. The executable high-evidence rule is Bench-authored.
